\chapter{A Meal}
\label{ch:te-a-meal}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say I am having a meal in Telugu, using the word an earlier chapter already used and never explained.}

Say \te{భోజనం} \te{చేద్దాం}, explain \te{భోజనం} against everyday \te{తిండి} the way Chapter 32 first set them side by side, and apologise for a late meal with Chapter 9's \te{క్షమించండి}.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bhōjanaṁ]{\te{భోజనం} (bhōjanaṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}a meal,\textquotedblright{} a word this book named before it ever taught it}

\label{lesson:TE-C40-bhojanam}



\begin{quote}
Tea, then milk. This chapter's last word is not a drink — it is the meal you would sit down to with both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{భోజనం}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{భోజనం}} — \emph{bhōjanaṁ} — \textbf{a meal}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{భోజనం} \te{చేద్దాం}.} — \emph{bhōjanaṁ cēddāṁ.} — \textquotedblleft{}Let's eat\textquotedblright{} (literally, \textquotedblleft{}let's do a meal\textquotedblright{}).
\end{quote}

Chapter 32 already used this exact word, in passing, as the polite counterpart of native \textbf{\te{తిండి}} — without ever teaching it properly. This lesson finally does.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{భోజనం}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{भोजन}}, built on \textbf{\dv{भुज्}} (\emph{bhuj}), \textquotedblleft{}to enjoy, to partake of, to eat.\textquotedblright{} It sits above native \textbf{\te{తిండి}} the same way \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} sits above the everyday \textbf{-\te{అండి}} ending: a formal Sanskrit layer over a plain Dravidian floor. Chapter 37's \textbf{\te{కన్ను}} was a word this book had already used once, unglossed, inside an etymology note — this lesson does the very same thing for \textbf{\te{భోజనం}}, which Chapter 32 named without teaching.

If a meal runs late, Telugu reaches for Chapter 9's own word: \textbf{\te{భోజనం} \te{ఆలస్యం} \te{అయింది}, \te{క్షమించండి}} — \textquotedblleft{}the meal is late, sorry\textquotedblright{} — the same respectful \textbf{-\te{అండి}} ending that first met you on \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}}'s own everyday alternative.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bhōjanaṁ cēddāṁ\textquotedblright{} — let's eat
  \item native, then borrowed — \textquotedblleft{}tiṇḍi … bhōjanaṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the apology — \textquotedblleft{}bhōjanaṁ ālasyaṁ ayindi, kṣamin̄caṇḍi\textquotedblright{}
  \item the chapter — \textquotedblleft{}ṭī … pālu … bhōjanaṁ\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}let's eat.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Bhōjanaṁ cēddāṁ}.) Which earlier chapter already used \emph{bhōjanaṁ}, without teaching it as its own word? (\textbf{Chapter 32's} \emph{tinu} lesson.) Apologise for a late meal, using Chapter 9's word. (\emph{Bhōjanaṁ ālasyaṁ ayindi, kṣamin̄caṇḍi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
